title: Duryodhana in Maya's hall
hookLine: a prince walks through his cousins' dazzling new hall and leaves burning with envy; sutra 1.33 names the cure he never took
carry: friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity: the mind clears
tomorrow: when baby Hanuman fell, the whole world stopped breathing. why?
last: EKA TATTVA: ONE THING, RETURNED TO.

lines: A FALL INTO THE POOL. LAUGHTER.
I'M BURNING. I CAN'T BEAR IT.
cards: In the Mahabharata, the Pandava brothers finally have a capital of their own, and the asura architect Maya builds them an assembly hall full of illusions. Their cousin Duryodhana comes to see it.
He mistakes a crystal floor for water and lifts his clothes; then he takes real water for crystal and falls in. Bhima laughs out loud.
Duryodhana goes home and tells his uncle Shakuni: seeing their good fortune, I'm burning. I can't bear it.

teach.b: That envy leads to the dice game, and the dice game, in time, to the war. Patanjali names the cure Duryodhana never took.
Sutra 1.33 pairs four attitudes with four kinds of people. Maitri, friendliness, toward the happy. Karuna, compassion, toward those who suffer.

Mudita, gladness, toward the good. Upeksha, equanimity, toward those who do wrong. Cultivate these, the sutra says, and the mind becomes clear and settled: chitta prasadana, like water once the mud settles.
Duryodhana met his cousins' happiness with envy instead of friendliness, and the laughter with rage instead of equanimity, and his mind never cleared again.
Commentators read friendliness toward the happy as the answer to envy: their good news isn't your loss.
And equanimity toward wrongdoers isn't approval; it means not letting their wrong take over your mind. Notice the reason the sutra gives.
Not only that these are kind, though they are: they keep your own mind clear enough to practice.

Buddhists know the same four by another name, the brahma viharas, and practice them too; in the Yoga Sutras, the stated fruit is a settled mind. Today, it's the group chat the moment a friend gets the thing you wanted.

how: Many yoga teachers present sutra 1.33 as a daily practice for relationships, consciously meeting the happy with friendliness, the suffering with compassion, the good with gladness and wrongdoers with equanimity.

o: goodwill saved for close friends only
maitri: goodwill toward people who are happy

games.q: the four attitudes, each to its kind of person.

s: equanimity toward wrongdoers means approving of what they did
it means not letting their wrong take over your mind. approval isn't part of it.
in the Mahabharata, Duryodhana's envy at the Pandavas' good fortune leads toward the dice game
he tells Shakuni he can't bear their good fortune, and the game is planned.
the result of the four attitudes is chitta prasadana, a clear mind
the mind made calm and bright, like settled water.

games.q: a coworker gets the promotion you wanted, and they're thrilled. which key does sutra 1.33 hand you?
o: friendliness: their happiness isn't your loss.
games.why: maitri, friendliness, is the attitude toward the happy. it cuts envy at the root, the envy that burned Duryodhana.

practice: Bring to mind someone happy right now, maybe someone who got what you wanted, and let a little friendliness rise. Then someone suffering, and let compassion come; then someone who did good, and be glad.
Then, gently, someone who did wrong, and let your mind stay level, not agreeing, not boiling. If you pray, hold each one before God for a breath. Then come back to the breath and notice the water.

wordCard.voice: Friendliness. Maitri, the first of the four attitudes in sutra 1.33, offered to the happy: the thing Duryodhana couldn't find in Maya's hall.

orig.note: Sanskrit maitrī: friendliness, goodwill; from mitra, friend. the first of the four attitudes in 1.33.

carryVoice: Your line: friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity, and the mind clears. One for each kind of person. See you tomorrow.
